title: Folio from a Qur'an Manuscript
medium: Ink, gold, and opaque watercolor on paper

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Louis E. and Theresa S. Seley Purchase Fund for Islamic Art and Rogers Fund, 1996

altText: A small page from a handwritten Qur'an on paper. Lines of Arabic calligraphy in ink are set on the page together with gold and colored decoration of the kind made of scrolling plants and geometric patterns.

context: A page from a Qur'an completed in 1137 in Iran by the calligrapher Muhammad al-Zanjani, from Zanjan. The Met describes the script as mainly eastern kufic with some cursive elements, and the manuscript's decoration as foliate scrolls and geometric interlace.

descriptions.k: This is a page from a very old book. The book is the Qur'an, a holy book for Muslims. The words are written by hand in beautiful letters. Gold and pretty patterns decorate the page. Trace a line of writing with your finger.
descriptions.g12: This page comes from a Qur'an, the holy book of Islam, made by hand almost 900 years ago in Iran. A skilled writer called a calligrapher wrote the words in ink. Gold and patterns decorate the page. Look at how even and careful the letters are. How long might it take to write one page?
descriptions.g35: This page is from a Qur'an, the holy book of Islam, copied by hand in Iran in 1137 by Muhammad al-Zanjani, a scribe from Zanjan. The Met says the letters are mainly in a style called eastern kufic, with some cursive touches. The manuscript is also decorated with gold, scrolling plants, and geometric patterns. Why do you think so much care was put into writing and decorating a holy book?
descriptions.g68: Muslims treat the Qur'an with great respect, and calligraphers have long made copies as acts of skill and devotion. This folio, part of a manuscript completed in 1137 by Muhammad al-Zanjani of Zanjan, is written mainly in eastern kufic with some cursive elements. The Met notes illumination with foliate scrolls and geometric interlace, using ink, gold, and opaque watercolor on paper. How do the writing and decoration share the page, and what does the care taken suggest about the text's importance?
descriptions.g910: This folio belongs to a Qur'an completed in 1137 in Iran and signed by the calligrapher Muhammad al-Zanjani. The script is mainly eastern kufic with some cursive elements, and the Met describes the decoration as foliate scrolls and geometric interlace. In Islamic art, calligraphy of the Qur'an is among the most honored arts, and here the shape of the letters, spacing, and ornament work as a unified design. Consider how script and illumination support each other without competing, and what the use of gold adds.
descriptions.g1112: As a dated work by a named calligrapher, this folio documents a moment in the development of the Qur'anic script in 12th-century Iran. The Met describes a mainly eastern kufic hand with cursive elements, and illumination of foliate scrolls and geometric interlace in ink, gold, and opaque watercolor on paper. The text is sacred, so its presentation is shaped by reverence as well as artistry. For viewers who cannot read Arabic, the page invites attention to rhythm, proportion, and ornament, while recognizing that its meaning and use extend far beyond visual appreciation.

g35.texture: How might ink on paper differ from gold paint in how it looks or feels?

g910.daily: How does the folio merge script, ornament, and sacred purpose in a single visual system?

g1112.daily: What can be argued from this folio about the relationship between sacred text and visual form, and what lies beyond what the image shows?
g1112.emotion: How do formal qualities of order and refinement mediate a viewer's emotional response to a sacred text?
g1112.observation: Describe the page's visual structure precisely, then consider how knowing its religious function changes your description.
g1112.analysis: Evaluate how the calligraphy and illumination are integrated, and where one may take precedence.
g1112.line: How does the calligrapher's control of line turn script into both text and abstract pattern?
g1112.shape: Discuss how foliate and geometric ornaments, as the Met describes them, structure the page differently from the script.
g1112.color: How might the limited, high-value palette of ink, gold, and opaque watercolor signal the manuscript's status?
g1112.texture: In what ways might the materiality of paper, ink, and gold shape the experience of a handwritten Qur'an?
g1112.space: How does the layout create a rhythm of reading, and how does it differ from the layout of a modern printed page?
g1112.light: How does the reflectivity of gold complicate the use of photographs as evidence of how this page looks?
g1112.meaning: Some viewers see calligraphy as a form of devotion. How might that understanding shape what counts as a successful page?
g1112.culture: What can a dated and signed Qur'an from 1137 tell us about book production and the transmission of scripts in Iran?
g1112.technique: How does the mix of eastern kufic and cursive elements indicate the development of calligraphic styles in the 12th century?
g1112.personal: How does your own literacy shape what you see here, and what responsibilities come with interpreting a sacred text visually?
g1112.critical: What are the ethical issues of displaying separated pages of a sacred book in a museum, and how might they be addressed?

teacherNote.context: A page from a Qur'an completed in 1137 in Iran by Muhammad al-Zanjani. The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam, and calligraphy is one of the most honored arts in Islamic culture.
directions: Have students practice slow, careful copying of a short phrase in their own script to feel the discipline of calligraphy.
Discuss how different communities treat sacred texts and how museums should respect that.
Compare this folio with the other Qur'an folio in the archive, noting differences in script, material, and decoration.
